claims.text: As-received Q235 steel contains a heterogeneous distribution of cementite or micro-carbide precipitates.
Annealing Q235 steel at 700 °C for 1–2 hours with controlled cooling will refine its microstructure.
The specified annealing treatment will homogenize the distribution of cementite or micro-carbide precipitates in Q235 steel.
The resulting precipitates will be uniformly distributed at grain boundaries and within the ferrite matrix.
Fine cementite or micro-carbide precipitates provide preferential nucleation sites for iron oxide formation.
A uniform precipitate distribution promotes spatially uniform oxide nucleation.
The refined microstructure enhances grain-boundary diffusion at high temperature.
Enhanced grain-boundary diffusion supports rapid formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale in aggressive salt at high temperature.
The oxide scale formed on annealed Q235 steel can self-heal minor defects.
A continuous, adherent, self-healing oxide scale reduces corrosion degradation of Q235 steel.
The coarser and inhomogeneous precipitate distribution in as-received Q235 steel produces an uneven oxide scale.
The uneven oxide scale on as-received Q235 steel is more prone to spallation and accelerated corrosion.
After Na2SO4–V2O5 exposure at approximately 800 °C for 24 hours, annealed Q235 steel will have lower weight gain than as-received Q235 steel.
After high-temperature salt exposure, annealed Q235 steel will exhibit less oxide-scale spallation than as-received Q235 steel.
After high-temperature salt exposure, annealed Q235 steel will form a more continuous oxide layer than as-received Q235 steel.
After high-temperature salt exposure, annealed Q235 steel will form a more adherent oxide layer than as-received Q235 steel.
At room temperature, diffusion is too slow for annealing-induced microstructural differences to produce significant corrosion differences.
Annealed and as-received Q235 steel will display similar corrosion behavior in the room-temperature salt environment.
The proposed protective effect should be significant only near 800 °C, where diffusion processes are active.
